hindi: माना कि $k$ वह धनात्मक पूर्णांक है जिसके लिए
solution: With $t=\tan x$: an antiderivative is $F(x)=\frac13\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan x}{3}\right)$, but $F$ jumps at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+m\pi$, so it may be used only on intervals free of these points
The integrand $g$ has period $\pi$ and $g(\pi-x)=g(x)$, so every interval $[\frac{m\pi}{2},\frac{(m+1)\pi}{2}]$ contributes $\frac{\pi}{6}$
solution_full: Let $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sin^{2}x+9\cos^{2}x}$, continuous and positive on $\mathbb{R}$. Dividing by $\cos^{2}x$: $g(x)=\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{\tan^{2}x+9}$, so on each interval where $\cos x\neq0$ an antiderivative is $F(x)=\dfrac13\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{3}\right)$.

$F$ is not continuous on $\mathbb{R}$: as $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^{-}$, $F\to\frac{\pi}{6}$, while as $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^{+}$, $F\to-\frac{\pi}{6}$. So $F(b)-F(a)$ is valid only when $[a,b]$ contains no point $\frac{\pi}{2}+m\pi$.

Since $g(\pi-x)=g(x)$, $\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}g=\int_0^{\pi/2}g=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; since $g(x+\pi)=g(x)$, the pattern repeats. So every interval $\left[\frac{m\pi}{2},\frac{(m+1)\pi}{2}\right]$ contributes $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\int_0^{k\pi/2}g=\dfrac{k\pi}{6}$.

Using $F\left(\frac{k\pi}{2}\right)-F(0)$ directly would give $0$ for even $k$ and $\pm\frac{\pi}{6}$ for odd $k$, which is wrong because $F$ jumps by $-\frac{\pi}{3}$ at each odd multiple of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
originality_note: New: the unknown is the upper limit k, so the student must count how many quarter-periods the integral covers while the obvious antiderivative resets at every pole of tan x (way 5). Closest known: int_0^{2pi} dx/(a + b cos x) with the half-angle antiderivative jump. Different because: the answer is a count of pieces and a naive antiderivative gives a k-independent value.
blueprint_concepts: Evaluation via the antiderivative; handling discontinuous antiderivatives

concept_use.Evaluation via the antiderivative; handl: The antiderivative (1/3) tan^-1((tan x)/3) is discontinuous at odd multiples of pi/2; the integral must be taken piece by piece, each quarter giving pi/6.

stem_review: Read as a student: the integrand is continuous and positive, so k is unique; numerical integration over 21 quarter-periods gives 7 pi/2 exactly. Answer 21, a positive 2-digit integer as planned. Changed: No change.
key_step: Each interval of length pi/2 contributes pi/6; the antiderivative (1/3) tan^-1(tan x/3) cannot be used across x = pi/2 + m pi.
justification: Routine once the discontinuity of the antiderivative is noticed: one substitution, one quarter-period value, a count. Above 2026-P2-Q4 (L1) because of the discontinuity trap and the counting.
